8.	Proto-Germanic, the ancestor language of English, German, Dutch, and the Scandinavian languages, had a word X meaning “a short garment” — typically a knee-length tunic worn by both sexes. Around the 5th century CE, the Anglo-Saxon dialect of this language softened the original “sk-“ sound at the start of many words to “sh-.” But the related dialect spoken in Scandinavia did not undergo this softening. For about 400 years, English speakers used only their version. Then, in the 9th and 10th centuries, Vikings from Denmark and Norway invaded and settled large parts of England, bringing their version of the same word into close contact with the English version. The two ended up coexisting in the language, but their meanings split: the Old English form became Y, now referring to the upper garment, while the Old Norse form became Z, now referring to the lower garment. ID Y (10 points) and Z (10 points).

Answers: Y=shirt from Old English, Z=skirt from Old Norse. Other doublets that English acquired in the same way during the Viking age include ship/skip, shatter/scatter, and shriek/screech — in each case, the "sh-" word is from Old English and the "sk-" word is from Old Norse.
